section_1.title: The Hook: The Constant Ratio
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of a constant ratio. Start with the intuition that regardless of a circle's size, its perimeter and diameter always scale proportionally. We define π as the ratio of Circumference (C) to Diameter (d).
section_1.example: Visual: An animation showing a tiny hamster wheel and a giant Ferris wheel. Both are rolled out to a flat line; both travel exactly π times their diameter distance in one rotation.

section_2.title: Historical Evolution: The Polygon Method
section_2.content: Explain how ancient mathematicians (Archimedes) estimated π without computers. They used the 'Method of Exhaustion'—inscribing and circumscribing polygons inside and outside a circle. As the number of sides increases, the polygon's perimeter approaches the circle's circumference.
section_2.example: Visual: A square inside a circle morphs into a hexagon, then a 12-sided, then a 100-sided polygon, visibly 'hugging' the circle tighter as the gap between the shape and the curve vanishes.

section_3.title: Formalizing π: Irrationality and Beyond
section_3.content: Define π mathematically as an irrational, transcendental number (3.14159...). Briefly explain that it never terminates and never settles into a repeating pattern, distinguishing it from simple fractions like 22/7.
section_3.example: Visual: A digital 'slot machine' showing decimals of π spinning rapidly and never stopping, compared to 22/7 which shows a simple repeating block.

section_4.title: Practical Application: Why π Matters
section_4.content: Connect the abstract number to real-world technology. Explain that π is essential for anything involving rotation, waves, or cycles—from GPS satellite positioning to the engineering of gears in a robot.
section_4.example: Visual: A robot arm picking up a soda can. The movement path is calculated using circular arcs that rely on the precision of π; an error in the decimal place would cause the arm to miss the target.

section_5.title: Summary and Conclusion
section_5.content: Recap: π = C/d. It is a bridge between the physical shape of a circle and infinite numerical complexity. Encourage curiosity about the 'infinite' nature of the number.
section_5.example: Visual: A 'Galaxy of Numbers' graphic where the digits of π spiral out to form the shape of a circle, reinforcing the theme of infinite geometry.
